Qobyz is a bowed lute of the Turkic peoples — Kazakh, Karakalpak, Bashkir and Tatar — and a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-7. The traditional qyl-qobyz has two strings and no frets; the body is carved from a single block, with the lower half of the resonator covered in skin and the upper half open, and the horsehair strings stand clear of the neck. The player holds the instrument upright and sounds the strings by touching them with the fingers rather than pressing them against a fingerboard, and the bow is of horsehair too. It was once played by shamans and traditional mediums in ritual, and it also accompanies Karakalpak epic singing.
傳統演奏時將琴身垂直持握，琴弦懸離琴頸，不以按壓指板取音，而以手指接觸弦、配合弓: In traditional playing the instrument is held upright, with the strings standing away from the neck; pitch is not set by pressing the strings against a fingerboard but by touching them with the fingers, using bow pressure and angle to change pitch, ornaments, harmonics and timbre. The bow is usually of horsehair, and the basic order of actions is to hold the instrument, bring the bow to the string, then adjust the pressure and the angle of the bow to separate the low register from the high harmonics. In the Karakalpak tradition the technique is mostly passed on within families, from master to pupil, in workshops or through formal teaching, and it serves to accompany narrative singing, to hold a drone and to play instrumental melody.

庫布茲傳統琴身多以整塊木料製成，常見胡桃木或樺木，琴頸無品；共鳴箱上半部開放，下: The traditional qobyz body is usually made from a single block of wood, commonly walnut or birch, with a fretless neck; the upper half of the resonator is open and the lower half is covered with animal skin — goatskin, camel calf skin or sheepskin are recorded. The strings are braided horsehair, and other accounts mention an early single horsehair or ox-tendon string, and three strings of camel tendon. The bow is of horsehair as well. Some historical instruments have metal pendants or small metal plates inside the soundbox. Improved versions have a pine soundboard, python or sheepskin, a fingerboard and four steel strings. The materials of the tuning pegs and other parts are not given.
庫布茲為古代突厥擦弦樂器，流傳於哈薩克、卡拉卡爾帕克、巴什基爾與韃靼等地，柯爾克: The qobyz is an ancient Turkic bowed instrument, found in Kazakhstan, Karakalpakstan, Bashkortostan and Tatarstan among other places; the Kyrgyz variant is called the kyl-kiyak. Traditionally it is bound up with shamanic and baksy ritual, and its origin legend is linked to Korkut Ata, though the date cannot be established. In the 1930s Soviet Kazakh folk orchestras brought out an improved version with four metal strings; the traditional two-string instrument declined for a time because of its ritual character and was revived from the 1960s and 70s. In Karakalpakstan the zhirau still use it for epic singing, and in 2025 it was inscribed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding.
庫布茲為弦鳴樂器，以馬尾弦擦奏，見於哈薩克、卡拉卡爾帕克、巴什基爾與韃靼等突厥語: The qobyz is a chordophone sounded with horsehair strings and a bow, found among Turkic-speaking peoples: Kazakh, Karakalpak, Bashkir and Tatar. Traditionally it is played in shamanic ritual and by the baksy (ritual musicians), and it also accompanies epics and dastans; the Karakalpak zhirau (epic singers) use it to colour the narrative, to play along with the voice or to bow a single note throughout. In the Soviet period it entered folk instrument orchestras, where the improved four-string version can play Kazakh music and violin repertoire; today it is also heard in folk ensembles, as a solo instrument, in ensemble and as accompaniment, and there are short kui pieces that imitate birdsong, animal calls and horses' hooves.
庫布茲為無品擦弦魯特琴，兩條馬尾弦不靠指板按壓，而以手指接觸弦發音；共鳴箱下半蒙: The qobyz is a fretless bowed lute: its two horsehair strings are not pressed against a fingerboard but sounded by the fingers touching them, and the lower half of the resonator is covered with skin while the upper half is open. The player makes ornaments, harmonics and contrasting colours with finger pressure and bow weight; the pressure and angle of the bow can bring out the denser low register or draw out higher harmonics. Historical instruments sometimes carry metal pendants that add an idiophonic sound as they move. Modernised versions have four metal strings, a range of up to two octaves and a tone closer to the violin. Unlike the plucked dombra, the qobyz sounds by friction from the bow; being fretless, with the strings far from the neck, it is also stopped differently from the usual bowed lutes with a fingerboard. Sources do not state clearly how the volume is controlled.
